taxonomy.subtopic: RANKL-dependent osteoclast differentiation and denosumab

questions.stem_html: A 69-year-old woman is evaluated after a low-trauma vertebral compression fracture. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry shows a femoral-neck T score of −3.0. She cannot tolerate oral bisphosphonates and begins treatment with a monoclonal antibody administered every 6 months. The accompanying diagram shows signaling between an osteoblast-lineage cell and an osteoclast precursor. Which process is most directly inhibited by this therapy?

options.text_html: Direct stimulation of osteoblast Wnt signaling by neutralization of sclerostin
Interruption of RANKL binding to RANK on osteoclast precursors
Irreversible incorporation into hydroxyapatite followed by osteoclast apoptosis
Activation of the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid chief cells
Selective estrogen-receptor agonism in breast and endometrial tissue

questions.explanation_html: Denosumab binds RANK ligand (RANKL), preventing RANKL from activating RANK on osteoclast precursors and mature osteoclasts. This decreases osteoclast formation, function, and survival, thereby reducing bone resorption. The mechanism is extracellular and reversible; the antibody is not incorporated into bone matrix.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Neutralization of sclerostin is the mechanism of romosozumab, an anabolic osteoporosis therapy that enhances Wnt signaling.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Bisphosphonates bind bone mineral and are taken up by osteoclasts; denosumab does not become incorporated into hydroxyapatite.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Calcimimetics activate the calcium-sensing receptor and reduce parathyroid hormone secretion; they are not the monoclonal therapy described.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Raloxifene is a selective estrogen-receptor modulator and is not administered as a six-monthly monoclonal antibody.

questions.educational_objective: Denosumab decreases bone resorption by blocking RANKL–RANK signaling required for osteoclast differentiation, activity, and survival.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing osteoblast-lineage RANKL signaling to RANK on an osteoclast precursor and blockade by denosumab.

taxonomy.subtopic: Encapsulated pneumococcal clearance by opsonization and splenic phagocytosis

questions.stem_html: A 72-year-old man who underwent splenectomy after trauma develops fever, pleuritic chest pain, and rust-colored sputum. Chest imaging shows dense consolidation of the right lower lobe. Blood cultures grow lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci that are alpha-hemolytic and optochin-sensitive. The accompanying schematic highlights the organism’s thick surface layer. Which immune process is most important for clearing this pathogen from the bloodstream?

options.text_html: Direct lysis of the organism by membrane attack complex assembly
Neutralization of pneumolysin by secretory IgA in the alveolar space
Recognition of peptidoglycan by cytosolic NOD2 in erythrocytes
Antibody- and complement-mediated opsonization of the polysaccharide capsule
Activation of eosinophils by parasite-specific IgE

questions.explanation_html: Streptococcus pneumoniae has an antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule. Type-specific antibodies and complement fragments, especially C3b, coat the capsule and permit recognition by phagocyte complement and Fc receptors. The spleen is particularly important for removing opsonized encapsulated organisms from blood, so asplenia markedly increases the risk of invasive pneumococcal disease.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: The membrane attack complex is most effective against susceptible gram-negative organisms; pneumococci are cleared primarily by opsonophagocytosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Mucosal IgA contributes to airway defense but does not replace splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria from the bloodstream.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Erythrocytes do not perform the phagocytic clearance required here, and NOD2 sensing is not the key protective mechanism against the capsule.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: IgE-driven eosinophil responses are important in helminth defense and allergy, not invasive pneumococcal bacteremia.

questions.educational_objective: The pneumococcal polysaccharide capsule impairs direct phagocytosis; antibody and C3b opsonization followed by splenic macrophage clearance is essential for protection against invasive disease.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing antibody and C3b coating a pneumococcal capsule and recognition by a splenic macrophage.

taxonomy.subtopic: Mu-receptor signaling and respiratory depression

questions.stem_html: A 58-year-old man with chronic back pain is found difficult to arouse after applying two fentanyl patches and taking an unfamiliar sleep medication. Respirations are 6/min, pupils are pinpoint, and arterial carbon dioxide tension is markedly elevated. The accompanying tracing shows progressive loss of ventilatory response to carbon dioxide. Which molecular action most directly produced this patient’s respiratory depression?

options.text_html: Activation of Gi-coupled μ receptors that opens potassium channels and closes presynaptic calcium channels
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Antagonism of NMDA receptors in the medullary respiratory center
Stimulation of Gs-coupled receptors that increases cyclic AMP in locus coeruleus neurons
Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral nociceptors

questions.explanation_html: μ-Opioid receptors are Gi/o-coupled. Their activation inhibits adenylyl cyclase, opens postsynaptic potassium channels, and closes presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Reduced excitability and neurotransmitter release in medullary respiratory networks blunt the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide. Naloxone competitively reverses this receptor-mediated effect.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition causes cholinergic excess rather than the classic opioid triad of CNS depression, miosis, and hypoventilation.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: NMDA antagonism is associated with drugs such as ketamine; it is not the principal mechanism of fentanyl respiratory depression.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: μ-receptor activation inhibits rather than stimulates adenylyl cyclase through Gi/o signaling.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Peripheral sodium-channel blockade describes local anesthetic action and does not explain profound central hypoventilation.

questions.educational_objective: μ-Opioid receptor activation engages Gi/o signaling, hyperpolarizes neurons, reduces transmitter release, and suppresses medullary responsiveness to carbon dioxide.

media.alt_text: Original diagram linking Gi-coupled mu-opioid signaling to a depressed ventilatory response to carbon dioxide.

taxonomy.subtopic: Meningococcal lipooligosaccharide and fulminant inflammatory shock

questions.stem_html: A 19-year-old college student develops fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash. Cerebrospinal fluid contains neutrophils, elevated protein, and low glucose; Gram stain shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci. Within hours, the patient becomes hypotensive with diffuse intravascular coagulation. The accompanying pathway diagram shows an outer-membrane glycolipid engaging an innate immune receptor complex. Which interaction most directly initiates the cytokine surge in this condition?

options.text_html: Binding of superantigen to the lateral surfaces of MHC class II and T-cell receptors
Activation of the alternative complement pathway by fungal beta-glucan
Cytosolic sensing of double-stranded viral RNA by MDA5
Cross-linking of Fc epsilon receptors on mast cells by allergen-specific IgE
CD14–MD-2–TLR4 recognition of meningococcal lipooligosaccharide

questions.explanation_html: Neisseria meningitidis releases lipooligosaccharide (LOS), a potent endotoxin. LOS binds the CD14–MD-2–TLR4 receptor complex on monocytes and macrophages, triggering NF-κB-dependent production of TNF, IL-1, and other mediators. The resulting endothelial activation, capillary leak, vasodilation, and coagulation activation can cause purpura fulminans and shock.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Superantigen-mediated T-cell activation is characteristic of toxic shock syndromes, not meningococcal endotoxemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Fungal beta-glucan is recognized primarily through receptors such as dectin-1 and does not explain meningococcal shock.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: MDA5 is a cytosolic viral RNA sensor and is unrelated to extracellular meningococcal LOS recognition.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Fcε-receptor cross-linking drives immediate hypersensitivity, not the endotoxin-triggered septic response described.

questions.educational_objective: Meningococcal lipooligosaccharide activates the CD14–MD-2–TLR4 complex, initiating NF-κB-dependent cytokine release, endothelial injury, shock, and DIC.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing meningococcal lipooligosaccharide binding CD14, MD-2, and TLR4 with downstream cytokine release.

taxonomy.subtopic: Hashimoto thyroiditis and Hürthle-cell metaplasia

questions.stem_html: A 43-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and a painless firm goiter. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is elevated, free thyroxine is low, and thyroid peroxidase antibodies are present. The accompanying thyroid section shows lymphoid follicles with germinal centers and large polygonal cells containing granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. These large cells are best described as which of the following?

options.text_html: Parafollicular C cells undergoing amyloid-producing neoplastic transformation
Thyroglossal duct remnants containing ectopic squamous epithelium
Follicular epithelial cells with mitochondrial proliferation after chronic injury
Activated macrophages containing ingested colloid and hemosiderin
Metastatic renal clear cells accumulating cytoplasmic lipid and glycogen

questions.explanation_html: The large eosinophilic cells are Hürthle cells, which are metaplastic thyroid follicular epithelial cells. Chronic autoimmune injury produces abundant mitochondrial accumulation, giving the cytoplasm its granular eosinophilic appearance. Hashimoto thyroiditis also features lymphocytic infiltration, germinal centers, and progressive follicular destruction.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Amyloid-producing parafollicular C-cell neoplasia describes medullary thyroid carcinoma, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Thyroglossal duct remnants are developmental midline lesions and do not create diffuse Hürthle-cell change.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Hürthle cells are epithelial cells with abundant mitochondria, not hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Metastatic clear-cell renal carcinoma has clear lipid- and glycogen-rich cytoplasm rather than granular eosinophilic Hürthle morphology.

questions.educational_objective: Hürthle cells in Hashimoto thyroiditis are metaplastic follicular epithelial cells packed with mitochondria because of chronic autoimmune injury.

media.alt_text: Original thyroid histology schematic showing lymphoid follicles and enlarged mitochondria-rich Hürthle cells.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and platelet activation

questions.stem_html: A 67-year-old woman receives unfractionated heparin after hip surgery. On hospital day 7, her platelet count falls from 246,000/mm³ to 92,000/mm³ and she develops a painful swollen calf. The accompanying chart shows the platelet trajectory and onset of thrombosis. Which mechanism best explains the simultaneous thrombocytopenia and prothrombotic state?

options.text_html: Autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 causing persistence of ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers
Drug-dependent antibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa causing isolated platelet destruction
Consumption of platelets and coagulation factors due to diffuse tissue-factor exposure alone
IgG binding PF4–heparin complexes and cross-linking platelet Fc gamma RIIa receptors
Antibodies against intrinsic factor causing ineffective hematopoiesis

questions.explanation_html: Immune HIT is caused by IgG antibodies against complexes of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin. Immune complexes cross-link FcγRIIa receptors on platelets, causing platelet activation, release of procoagulant microparticles, thrombin generation, and further PF4 release. Platelets are consumed, but thrombosis—not bleeding—is the dominant clinical danger.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, usually with microangiopathic hemolysis rather than the timed heparin-associated syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Some drugs cause immune platelet destruction, but isolated clearance does not explain HIT's intense thrombin generation and thrombosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Disseminated intravascular coagulation consumes factors and platelets; the heparin timing and new thrombosis instead point to PF4-dependent platelet activation.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Intrinsic-factor antibodies cause vitamin B12 deficiency and do not produce an acute prothrombotic platelet fall.

questions.educational_objective: HIT results from IgG recognition of PF4–heparin complexes with FcγRIIa-mediated platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, and marked thrombin generation.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing a day 5 to 10 platelet fall and PF4-heparin immune complexes activating platelets.

taxonomy.subtopic: Antral H pylori, D-cell suppression, and acid hypersecretion

questions.stem_html: A 38-year-old man has recurrent epigastric pain that improves temporarily after meals. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer, and a urea breath test is positive. The accompanying diagram compares antral G-cell and D-cell signaling before and after infection. Which change most directly promotes the high duodenal acid load in this patient?

options.text_html: Stimulation of parietal-cell acid secretion by secretin
Reduced antral somatostatin signaling with secondary hypergastrinemia
Destruction of chief cells with loss of pepsinogen secretion
Autoantibody-mediated blockade of histamine H2 receptors
Inhibition of the gastric proton pump by bacterial ammonia

questions.explanation_html: Antral-predominant H pylori gastritis reduces somatostatin output from D cells and increases gastrin release from G cells. Gastrin stimulates enterochromaffin-like cells to release histamine and also promotes parietal-cell acid secretion. The resulting increased acid delivery to the duodenum contributes to gastric metaplasia and duodenal ulcer formation.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Secretin inhibits gastric acid secretion and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate rather than driving the high-acid state.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Chief-cell injury would reduce pepsinogen but is not the principal endocrine mechanism of H pylori–associated duodenal ulceration.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: H2-receptor blockade would decrease acid output; autoantibodies against this receptor are not the mechanism described.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Bacterial urease-derived ammonia supports local survival but does not function as a proton-pump inhibitor causing hyperacidity.

questions.educational_objective: Antral H pylori infection suppresses D-cell somatostatin, increases gastrin, and raises gastric acid delivery to the duodenum.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing antral H pylori reducing D-cell somatostatin and increasing G-cell gastrin and acid secretion.

taxonomy.subtopic: Diffuse radioactive iodine uptake in Graves disease

questions.stem_html: A 31-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, palpitations, a diffuse nontender goiter, and bilateral proptosis. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is undetectable. The accompanying radioactive iodine image shows intense homogeneous uptake throughout both thyroid lobes. Which process best explains the scan despite suppression of pituitary TSH?

options.text_html: Autonomous secretion of thyroxine by a single toxic adenoma
Release of stored hormone after painful subacute follicular destruction
Exogenous thyroid hormone suppressing endogenous iodine uptake
TSH-independent activation of cyclic AMP by a constitutively active Gs mutation in one nodule
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin acting as an agonist at the TSH receptor throughout the gland

questions.explanation_html: Graves disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that act as agonists at the TSH receptor on follicular cells. Receptor activation increases cyclic AMP, iodide uptake, hormone synthesis, and gland growth diffusely. Therefore uptake is high and homogeneous even though endogenous pituitary TSH is suppressed by negative feedback.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: A toxic adenoma produces focal uptake with suppression of the surrounding thyroid, not diffuse homogeneous uptake.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Subacute thyroiditis releases preformed hormone from damaged follicles and therefore produces low uptake.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Exogenous hormone suppresses TSH and endogenous thyroid activity, also producing low uptake.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: A constitutively active Gs pathway in a nodule produces focal autonomy rather than uniform stimulation of the entire gland.

questions.educational_objective: In Graves disease, TSH-receptor–stimulating antibodies drive diffuse iodide uptake and hormone synthesis despite suppressed pituitary TSH.

media.alt_text: Original schematic comparing diffuse Graves uptake with focal toxic nodule and low thyroiditis uptake patterns.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteremia as a marker of colorectal neoplasia

questions.stem_html: A 64-year-old man has several weeks of fatigue, low-grade fever, and a new regurgitant murmur. Echocardiography shows an aortic-valve vegetation. Multiple blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus. He has no abdominal symptoms and fecal occult blood testing is negative. The accompanying schematic links the bloodstream isolate to a potential mucosal source. Which evaluation is most appropriate after stabilization of the cardiac infection?

options.text_html: Colonoscopy to evaluate for colorectal adenoma or carcinoma
Bronchoscopy to exclude an occult central lung tumor
Bone marrow biopsy to evaluate for plasma-cell neoplasia
Renal biopsy to evaluate for immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Temporal-artery biopsy to evaluate for giant-cell arteritis

questions.explanation_html: S gallolyticus bacteremia and endocarditis have a strong association with colorectal adenomas and carcinomas. Colonic neoplasia can disrupt the mucosal barrier and permit bacterial translocation, and the cardiac infection may be the first clinical clue. Colonoscopy is therefore indicated even when gastrointestinal symptoms and stool blood testing are absent.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: This organism is linked to colorectal rather than bronchogenic neoplasia.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Multiple myeloma is not the characteristic occult disease associated with S gallolyticus bacteremia.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Endocarditis can cause glomerular injury, but the key disease-screening association of this isolate is colorectal neoplasia.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Giant-cell arteritis is unrelated to this bloodstream organism and cardiac vegetation.

questions.educational_objective: S gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis should prompt colonoscopic evaluation because of its association with colorectal adenomas and carcinoma.

media.alt_text: Original schematic linking a colonic neoplastic lesion, bloodstream translocation of S gallolyticus, and a cardiac-valve vegetation.

taxonomy.subtopic: Lynch syndrome mismatch-repair deficiency and microsatellite instability

questions.stem_html: A 41-year-old woman is diagnosed with right-sided colon cancer. Her mother had endometrial cancer at age 44, and a maternal uncle had colon cancer at age 47. Tumor testing shows high microsatellite instability and loss of MSH2 and MSH6 staining. The accompanying DNA diagram shows repetitive sequences gaining and losing nucleotides during replication. Which repair process is defective?

options.text_html: Nucleotide-excision repair of bulky ultraviolet-induced thymine dimers
Base-excision repair of deaminated cytosine residues
Postreplicative correction of base mismatches and insertion-deletion loops
Nonhomologous end joining of ionizing-radiation double-strand breaks
Direct reversal of O6-methylguanine by methylguanine methyltransferase

questions.explanation_html: MSH2 and MSH6 form a mismatch-recognition complex in the DNA mismatch-repair pathway. Loss of mismatch repair permits persistence of base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops, especially in repetitive microsatellite sequences, producing microsatellite instability. Germline loss-of-function variants in mismatch-repair genes cause Lynch syndrome.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Nucleotide-excision repair removes bulky helix-distorting lesions and is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Base-excision repair handles small non-bulky base lesions and does not explain microsatellite instability with MSH2/MSH6 loss.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Nonhomologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks but is not the postreplicative mismatch pathway identified by the tumor staining.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: MGMT directly reverses a specific alkylation lesion and is unrelated to inherited mismatch-repair deficiency.

questions.educational_objective: Lynch syndrome results from germline mismatch-repair deficiency, causing persistence of replication errors and microsatellite instability.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing an insertion-deletion loop at a microsatellite and recognition by the MSH2-MSH6 mismatch-repair complex.

taxonomy.subtopic: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone blockade in HFrEF remodeling

questions.stem_html: A 59-year-old man has a large anterior myocardial infarction. Three months later, echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 32%. An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is added to his regimen. The accompanying diagram shows progressive chamber dilation driven by neurohormonal signaling. Which effect best explains the long-term benefit of this medication?

options.text_html: Selective slowing of atrioventricular nodal conduction without changing ventricular loading
Immediate dissolution of replacement fibrosis by activation of matrix metalloproteinases
Increased aldosterone secretion with expansion of intravascular volume
Direct opening of ATP-sensitive potassium channels in ventricular myocytes
Reduction of angiotensin II– and aldosterone-mediated afterload, fibrosis, and ventricular remodeling

questions.explanation_html: ACE inhibition lowers angiotensin II and aldosterone signaling. This reduces systemic vascular resistance and sodium retention and also attenuates maladaptive myocyte hypertrophy, fibroblast activation, collagen deposition, and ventricular dilation. The benefit in HFrEF therefore extends beyond immediate blood-pressure reduction to limitation of progressive remodeling.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: AV-nodal slowing describes drugs such as beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers and does not capture ACE inhibitor remodeling benefit.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: ACE inhibitors reduce ongoing remodeling signals; they do not acutely dissolve established infarct scar.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: ACE inhibition decreases aldosterone signaling and sodium retention rather than increasing them.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: ATP-sensitive potassium-channel opening is not the principal mechanism of ACE inhibitors.

questions.educational_objective: ACE inhibition in HFrEF reduces afterload and suppresses angiotensin II– and aldosterone-driven hypertrophy, fibrosis, sodium retention, and ventricular dilation.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing reduced RAAS signaling, afterload, fibrosis, and ventricular dilation during ACE inhibition in HFrEF.

taxonomy.subtopic: Left atrial appendage stasis and cardioembolic stroke

questions.stem_html: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension has persistent atrial fibrillation. Transesophageal echocardiography shows spontaneous echo contrast and a small thrombus in the left atrial appendage. The accompanying flow map demonstrates markedly reduced appendage emptying velocity. Which component of Virchow’s triad is most directly responsible for thrombus formation?

options.text_html: Low-flow stasis within the left atrial appendage due to ineffective atrial contraction
High-velocity shear injury at the aortic valve causing platelet-rich thrombi
Paradoxical embolization through a patent ductus arteriosus
Direct endothelial invasion by atrial myocytes
Immune-complex deposition in left atrial endocardium

questions.explanation_html: Atrial fibrillation abolishes coordinated atrial contraction and creates low-velocity, recirculating flow in the left atrial appendage. This blood stasis is the dominant Virchow-triad mechanism for appendage thrombus and subsequent cardioembolic stroke. Structural atrial remodeling and endothelial dysfunction can add risk, but low flow is central.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: High shear is relevant to some arterial platelet-rich thrombi but does not explain left atrial appendage thrombosis during fibrillation.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Paradoxical embolization requires a venous thrombus and right-to-left shunt; a patent ductus usually produces left-to-right flow outside the neonatal period.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Atrial myocytes do not invade endocardium to generate thrombus.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Immune-complex endocardial deposition is not the primary mechanism of atrial-fibrillation thrombosis.

questions.educational_objective: Loss of coordinated atrial contraction in atrial fibrillation causes left atrial appendage blood stasis, promoting thrombus formation and cardioembolic stroke.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing atrial fibrillation, low left atrial appendage emptying velocity, stasis, and thrombus formation.

taxonomy.subtopic: BRCA1/BRCA2 and homologous recombination

questions.stem_html: A 34-year-old woman has triple-negative breast cancer. Her sister had ovarian cancer at age 39, and germline testing identifies a pathogenic BRCA1 variant. The accompanying diagram shows repair of a double-strand break using the intact sister chromatid as a template. Which cellular process is impaired in this patient’s cells?

options.text_html: Mismatch repair of single-base errors immediately after DNA replication
Nucleotide-excision repair of bulky ultraviolet photoproducts
Base-excision repair of oxidized purines
RAD51-mediated homologous recombination of double-strand DNA breaks
Telomerase-independent maintenance of chromosome ends

questions.explanation_html: BRCA1 and BRCA2 coordinate high-fidelity homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks. BRCA1 participates in damage sensing and pathway choice, while BRCA2 regulates loading of RAD51 onto single-stranded DNA. Loss of this pathway creates genomic instability and sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents and PARP inhibition.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Mismatch repair is associated with genes such as MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2 rather than BRCA1.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Nucleotide-excision repair removes bulky adducts and ultraviolet photoproducts and is not the BRCA pathway.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Base-excision repair handles small damaged bases through glycosylases and AP endonuclease.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Alternative lengthening of telomeres is not the central repair defect in hereditary BRCA-associated cancer.

questions.educational_objective: BRCA1 and BRCA2 preserve genomic stability by supporting RAD51-mediated homologous recombination of double-strand DNA breaks.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing BRCA1 and BRCA2 supporting RAD51 loading and sister-chromatid homologous recombination.

taxonomy.subtopic: Temporal-lobe encephalitis and hippocampal memory dysfunction

questions.stem_html: A 46-year-old man develops fever, seizures, bizarre behavior, and receptive-language difficulty. Cerebrospinal fluid contains lymphocytes and erythrocytes, and polymerase-chain-reaction testing is positive for HSV-1. The accompanying MRI schematic shows hemorrhagic abnormalities in the medial temporal lobes and insula. After recovery, which function is most likely to remain impaired?

options.text_html: Procedural memory for previously learned motor sequences
Formation of new declarative memories by medial temporal structures
Primary visual processing in the calcarine cortex
Initiation of voluntary movement by the primary motor cortex
Auditory localization by the superior olivary complex

questions.explanation_html: HSV-1 encephalitis characteristically involves the temporal lobes, often including the hippocampal formations. Bilateral medial temporal injury can produce profound anterograde amnesia with impaired consolidation of new declarative memories. Procedural learning relies more heavily on basal ganglia and cerebellar circuits.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Procedural motor learning depends mainly on basal ganglia and cerebellar circuits and is relatively distinct from hippocampal declarative memory.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: The calcarine cortex lies in the occipital lobe, not the medial temporal distribution highlighted.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Primary motor cortex injury causes contralateral weakness rather than the characteristic memory deficit.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: The superior olivary complex is in the brainstem and mediates binaural auditory localization.

questions.educational_objective: HSV encephalitis preferentially injures medial temporal and limbic structures; hippocampal damage impairs consolidation of new declarative memories.

media.alt_text: Original brain schematic highlighting hemorrhagic HSV involvement of medial temporal lobes and hippocampi.

taxonomy.subtopic: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma as a precursor of high-grade serous carcinoma

questions.stem_html: A 42-year-old woman with a pathogenic BRCA1 variant undergoes risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The ovaries are grossly normal, but microscopic examination of the fimbrial end of one tube shows a small focus of atypical cells with strong p53 staining and a high proliferative index. The accompanying diagram maps the lesion to the distal tube. These cells are the likely precursor of which common malignancy and arise from which cell type?

options.text_html: Granulosa cells of an antral follicle
Ovarian stromal theca interna cells
Secretory epithelium of the distal fallopian-tube fimbria
Endometrial stromal cells implanted on the ovary
Mesothelial cells of the broad ligament

questions.explanation_html: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) in the distal fallopian-tube fimbria is a recognized precursor of many high-grade serous carcinomas involving the ovary, tube, and peritoneum. The precursor is thought to arise from Müllerian secretory epithelial cells, particularly in individuals with BRCA-associated homologous-recombination deficiency.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Granulosa cells give rise to sex-cord stromal tumors, often associated with estrogen production.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Theca interna cells are steroidogenic stromal cells and are not the usual source of high-grade serous carcinoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Ectopic endometrial tissue is associated with endometriosis and some endometrioid or clear-cell tumors, not classic STIC.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Broad-ligament mesothelial cells are not the recognized precursor population for high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma.

questions.educational_objective: Many high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinomas originate from p53-abnormal secretory epithelium in the distal fallopian-tube fimbria, identifiable as STIC.

taxonomy.subtopic: Hepatorenal syndrome and effective arterial underfilling

questions.stem_html: A 55-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and tense ascites develops a progressive rise in serum creatinine. Urinalysis is bland, renal ultrasonography is normal, and kidney function does not improve after withdrawal of diuretics and albumin expansion. The accompanying hemodynamic diagram shows low systemic vascular resistance in the splanchnic bed and reduced renal blood flow. Which mechanism best explains the renal dysfunction?

options.text_html: Splanchnic arterial vasodilation with compensatory renal vasoconstriction and reduced effective arterial volume
Immune-complex deposition in glomerular capillary walls
Direct bilirubin toxicity causing diffuse cortical necrosis
Obstruction of collecting ducts by uric-acid crystals
Loss of antidiuretic hormone causing free-water depletion

questions.explanation_html: Advanced portal hypertension produces marked splanchnic arterial vasodilation. The resulting fall in effective arterial blood volume activates the sympathetic nervous system, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vasopressin. These responses produce intense renal vasoconstriction and reduced glomerular filtration despite structurally preserved kidneys, which is the core physiology of hepatorenal syndrome.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis would usually produce an active urine sediment and structural glomerular injury.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: The syndrome is primarily hemodynamic rather than diffuse toxic cortical necrosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Crystal obstruction would produce intrarenal injury and urinary findings rather than the classic bland-sediment, low-flow physiology.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Vasopressin is increased, not lost, in advanced cirrhosis and contributes to water retention and hyponatremia.

questions.educational_objective: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional decline in GFR caused by portal-hypertension–driven splanchnic vasodilation, effective arterial underfilling, and compensatory renal vasoconstriction.

taxonomy.subtopic: Monosodium urate activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome

questions.stem_html: A 52-year-old man awakens with severe pain, erythema, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial fluid contains needle-shaped crystals that are strongly negatively birefringent. The accompanying diagram shows a macrophage engulfing a crystal and releasing a mature cytokine that recruits neutrophils. Which intracellular event is required for production of this cytokine?

options.text_html: STAT6 activation with class switching to IgE
Alternative-pathway complement activation with membrane attack complex formation
NLRP3 assembly with caspase-1 cleavage of pro–interleukin-1 beta
RAG1-dependent V(D)J recombination in synovial B cells
Fas-mediated deletion of autoreactive neutrophils

questions.explanation_html: Monosodium urate crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammasome assembly activates caspase-1, which cleaves pro–IL-1β into mature IL-1β. IL-1β drives endothelial activation and intense neutrophil recruitment during an acute gout flare.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: STAT6 promotes type 2 immunity and IgE class switching and is not the urate-crystal inflammasome pathway.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Complement can amplify inflammation but does not perform the intracellular cleavage of pro–IL-1β asked about.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: V(D)J recombination generates antigen-receptor diversity in developing lymphocytes and is unrelated to acute crystal-induced inflammation.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Fas-mediated apoptosis does not generate mature IL-1β or initiate the neutrophilic gout flare.

questions.educational_objective: Monosodium urate crystals activate macrophage NLRP3, leading to caspase-1–mediated maturation of IL-1β and neutrophil-rich acute gout inflammation.

taxonomy.subtopic: EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma and tyrosine-kinase signaling

questions.stem_html: A 48-year-old woman who has never smoked is diagnosed with a peripheral lung adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing identifies an activating EGFR exon 19 deletion, and treatment with an EGFR tyrosine-kinase inhibitor is initiated. The accompanying pathway graphic shows reduced phosphorylation downstream of the receptor. Which action best describes the therapeutic effect?

options.text_html: Inhibition of a cytosolic serine-threonine receptor activated by transforming growth factor beta
Blockade of constitutive receptor tyrosine-kinase signaling through RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways
Covalent inhibition of DNA topoisomerase II in all rapidly dividing cells
Neutralization of vascular endothelial growth factor in the extracellular space only
Activation of p53-mediated apoptosis by inhibiting MDM2

questions.explanation_html: Activating EGFR variants produce ligand-independent receptor tyrosine-kinase activity and persistent signaling through pathways including RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT. EGFR tyrosine-kinase inhibitors suppress receptor autophosphorylation and downstream proliferative and survival signaling in susceptible tumors.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: TGF-β receptors have serine-threonine kinase activity, whereas EGFR is a membrane receptor tyrosine kinase.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Topoisomerase inhibition is a nonspecific cytotoxic mechanism and does not explain genotype-selected EGFR therapy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: VEGF neutralization describes antiangiogenic antibodies and is distinct from intracellular EGFR kinase inhibition.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: MDM2 inhibition is not the mechanism of standard EGFR tyrosine-kinase inhibitors.

questions.educational_objective: Activating EGFR variants drive lung adenocarcinoma through constitutive receptor tyrosine-kinase signaling; targeted inhibitors reduce downstream RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT activity.

taxonomy.subtopic: Monoclonal light-chain cast nephropathy

questions.stem_html: A 63-year-old man has fatigue, back pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, and multiple punched-out skull lesions. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike. Serum creatinine is elevated; a urine dipstick shows only trace protein, but total urinary protein is markedly increased. The accompanying nephron schematic shows intratubular fractured casts surrounded by giant cells. Which process most directly caused the kidney injury?

options.text_html: Selective albumin leakage through subepithelial immune-complex deposits
Renal-artery vasoconstriction caused by excess renin secretion
Urate precipitation caused by rapid spontaneous tumor lysis
Amyloid deposition limited to the renal pelvis
Filtered monoclonal light chains precipitating with tubular proteins to form obstructing casts

questions.explanation_html: Monoclonal free light chains are small enough to be filtered and can bind tubular proteins, including uromodulin, producing obstructing and directly toxic casts in distal nephron segments. Standard urine dipsticks primarily detect albumin and may underestimate light-chain proteinuria. This explains the discrepancy between trace dipstick protein and high total urinary protein.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Subepithelial immune-complex disease produces albumin-rich glomerular proteinuria that is readily detected by dipstick.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Renovascular disease does not explain the monoclonal protein, dipstick discrepancy, or fractured tubular casts.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Tumor-lysis nephropathy can produce uric-acid crystals but is not the characteristic cast lesion of untreated myeloma.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: AL amyloid can involve glomeruli and vessels, but deposition limited to the renal pelvis would not create these intratubular casts.

questions.educational_objective: Myeloma cast nephropathy results when filtered monoclonal light chains bind tubular proteins, forming obstructing and nephrotoxic casts that may be missed by albumin-focused urine dipsticks.

media.alt_text: Original graphic showing a monoclonal serum spike, filtered light chains, and fractured casts in distal nephron segments.

taxonomy.subtopic: Flecainide use-dependent sodium-channel blockade and rate-related QRS widening

questions.stem_html: A 45-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and no structural heart disease begins flecainide. His resting electrocardiogram shows mild QRS prolongation, but exercise testing produces substantially greater QRS widening at faster heart rates. The accompanying graph plots QRS duration against heart rate. Which property of the drug explains this finding?

options.text_html: Preferential blockade of potassium channels at slow heart rates, causing reverse use dependence
Irreversible antagonism of beta-1 receptors during sympathetic activation
Inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase with accumulation of intracellular calcium
Use-dependent blockade of activated cardiac sodium channels with slow recovery between beats
Selective blockade of L-type calcium channels in the atrioventricular node

questions.explanation_html: Flecainide is a class IC sodium-channel blocker with strong state and use dependence. It binds preferentially after channel activation and dissociates slowly during diastole. At faster rates, less time is available for recovery from block, so sodium-channel availability and ventricular conduction velocity decline progressively, producing greater QRS widening.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Reverse use dependence is more characteristic of some potassium-channel blockers whose repolarization effect is greater at slower rates.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Flecainide is not an irreversible beta blocker.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition is the mechanism of digoxin and primarily alters intracellular calcium and AV-nodal physiology.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: L-type calcium-channel blockade describes class IV agents and mainly affects nodal conduction rather than producing use-dependent ventricular QRS widening.

questions.educational_objective: Flecainide shows use-dependent class IC sodium-channel blockade; slow unbinding causes progressively greater conduction slowing and QRS widening at faster heart rates.
